lead: A reciprocating pump pushes water in bursts, so the delivery pipe sees a fast flow near mid-stroke and almost no flow near the dead centres. An air vessel is a closed branch on the pipe with trapped air. It stores water when the piston is fast and returns it when the piston is slow. The delivery flow becomes steadier and less energy is lost to pipe friction. You see air vessels on hand pumps, reciprocating feed pumps and old boiler-feed sets. This chapter finds the work saved against delivery friction for a single-acting pump.
prereq: You need: 7.7 for crank, piston and ideal flow, and Unit 4 for pipe friction.

blocks.text: In a single-acting pump the crank turns at constant angular speed ω, in rad/s. Let r be crank radius, in m; L = 2r is stroke, in m; A is piston area, in m²; and θ is crank angle from inner dead centre, in radians. The piston velocity is approximately v_p = ω r sin θ. The delivery flow is Q = A v_p = A ω r sin θ, in m³/s. It is zero at θ = 0 and θ = π, and maximum at mid-stroke.

Friction head in the delivery pipe follows Darcy–Weisbach: h_f = f L_p v²/(2 g D), where f is friction factor, L_p is pipe length, v is pipe velocity, D is pipe diameter and g is gravitational acceleration. Since v is proportional to Q, h_f varies as sin² θ. Let h_f,max be the friction head at peak delivery velocity. Then during delivery h_f = h_f,max sin² θ. The mean of sin² θ is 1/2, but work uses the integral of sin³ θ, not the mean head. That is the source of the 2/3 factor.
Q = A ω r sin θ;   h_f = h_f,max sin² θ
blocks.where: Q is delivery flow in m³/s; A is piston area in m²; ω is crank angular speed in rad/s; r is crank radius in m; θ is crank angle in radians; h_f is instantaneous friction head in m; h_f,max is friction head at peak delivery velocity in m.

blocks.text: An air vessel is a closed chamber connected by a branch pipe, as the figure shows. It holds trapped air above water. On the delivery side it is fitted close to the pump, before the long delivery pipe. On the suction side it can be fitted close to the pump on the suction pipe. The suction vessel reduces the acceleration head needed to start and stop the water column each stroke. The delivery vessel smooths the flow and cuts friction work.

items: Fast part of stroke: piston speed is high, Q is above mean, water rises in the vessel and compresses the trapped air.
Slow part of stroke: piston speed is low, Q is below mean, compressed air pushes stored water back into the delivery pipe.
Large vessel: air volume is big, so pressure change is small. Delivery-pipe flow stays nearly constant at the cycle mean Q_mean = A L N/60, where N is pump speed in rpm.

blocks.text: For a large delivery air vessel, the delivery pipe carries Q_mean all through the cycle. The friction head is then constant at h_f,max/π². Why π²? For single-acting simple harmonic motion, Q_mean = Q_max/π, and friction head goes as Q². A small vessel cannot hold pressure constant, so this result does not apply.
For one delivery stroke, without an air vessel, integrate power ρ g Q h_f over the stroke. The result for a single-acting pump is:
W_f = (2/3) ρ g A L h_f,max
blocks.where: W_f is friction work per stroke in J; ρ is water density in kg/m³; g is gravitational acceleration in m/s²; A is piston area in m²; L is stroke in m; h_f,max is peak friction head in m.

blocks.text: With a large air vessel the flow is steady at Q_mean and the friction head is h_f,max/π². The work per stroke becomes:
W_f,av = ρ g A L h_f,max / π²
blocks.where: W_f,av is friction work per stroke with a large air vessel in J; the other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: Saved work = W_f − W_f,av = (2/3 − 1/π²) ρ g A L h_f,max ≈ 0.565 ρ g A L h_f,max. The saving is about 84.8% of the no-vessel friction work. The air vessel does not change the useful pumping work; it changes only the friction loss in the pipe. It also protects the pipe from water hammer by reducing sudden velocity changes.

figure.caption: A branch air vessel sits on the delivery pipe. It stores water on the fast stroke and returns it on the slow stroke, so the delivery line sees a steadier flow. For the worked example, h_f,max = 6 m.

spec.title: Air vessel on delivery pipe
spec.aria: A branch air vessel on the delivery pipe stores water on the fast stroke and returns it on the slow stroke, giving steadier delivery.

examples.question: A single-acting reciprocating pump has cylinder area 0.03 m², stroke 0.30 m and speed 60 rpm. The maximum friction head in the delivery pipe is 6 m. Find the work done against friction per stroke without an air vessel and with a large air vessel, and the percentage saved. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Given: A = 0.03 m², L = 0.30 m, N = 60 rpm, h_f,max = 6 m, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Volume per stroke = A L = 0.03 × 0.30 = 0.009 m³.
Without air vessel: W_f = (2/3) × 529.74 = 353.16 J per stroke.
With large air vessel: W_f,av = 529.74 / π² = 529.74 / 9.8696 = 53.67 J per stroke.
examples.answer: The work against delivery friction is 353.16 J per stroke without an air vessel and 53.67 J with a large air vessel; the saving is 299.49 J per stroke, about 84.8%.
examples.check:
import math
rho = 1000
g = 9.81
A = 0.03
L = 0.30
N = 60
hf = 6
W_no = (2/3) * rho * g * A * L * hf
W_av = rho * g * A * L * hf / math.pi**2
saved = W_no - W_av
pct = 100 * saved / W_no
print(round(W_no, 2))
print(round(W_av, 2))
print(round(saved, 2))
print(round(pct, 1))

traps: Do not use mean friction head in the without-air-vessel work. h_f varies as sin² θ, so the factor is 2/3, not 1/2.
Do not apply the π² formula to a small air vessel or to the suction pipe. It is the large-delivery-vessel result for single-acting flow.
Keep h_f,max as the peak friction head. If the data gives an average head, convert using the definition in the question; do not guess.
The 84.8% is the fraction of friction work saved, not the fraction of total pump power saved.
A double-acting pump has two delivery strokes per revolution. The 2/3 and 1/π² factors change; use them only for single-acting unless the double-acting case is derived.

quiz.a: A closed chamber with trapped air, connected by a branch to a pump pipe. It stores water at high flow and returns it at low flow.

quiz.q: Why does delivery friction head vary as sin² θ in a single-acting pump?
quiz.a: Delivery flow Q varies as sin θ. Pipe friction head varies as v², and v is proportional to Q, so h_f varies as sin² θ.

quiz.q: A single-acting pump has A = 0.02 m², L = 0.25 m, h_f,max = 4 m, ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². Find the work saved by a large air vessel per stroke.
A pump has an air vessel on delivery but none on suction. Explain why delivery friction falls but suction acceleration head remains.
quiz.a: The delivery vessel keeps delivery-pipe flow nearly constant, so delivery friction is steady and low. The suction pipe still has to accelerate and decelerate its water column every stroke, so suction acceleration head is unchanged.

quiz.q: State the friction work per stroke with a large delivery air vessel for a single-acting pump.
quiz.a: W_f,av = ρ g A L h_f,max / π², where h_f,max is the peak friction head.

quiz.q: Why does a large air vessel make delivery flow nearly constant?
quiz.a: A large trapped-air volume changes little in pressure when water enters or leaves. The air cushion can absorb the fast-stroke excess and supply the slow-stroke deficit without a large pressure swing.

quiz.q: For h_f,max = 6 m and a large air vessel, what fraction of the no-vessel friction work remains?
quiz.a: W_f,av / W_f = (1/π²) / (2/3) = 3/(2π²) = 0.151. About 15.1% remains, so about 84.9% is saved.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern reciprocating pumps often use bladder or diaphragm dampers instead of open air vessels, because trapped air can dissolve into water and the cushion can be lost. Search for pulsation dampers, accumulator sizing and API 674 for reciprocating pump piping. In large pipelines, the same idea appears as a surge tank, which stores or releases water to control pressure waves.
